etymology: From a proper name, per the Oxford English Dictionary: the Scottish theologian John Duns Scotus (c. 1265/66–1308). The OED records its earliest evidence in 1530, in the Tyndale Bible. Its own third edition cites mid-sixteenth-century uses for a follower of Duns Scotus, for a person given to ridiculous pedantry, and for a fool.
biblical_def: A dunce is a person slow at learning, or plainly stupid. The word began as a theologian’s name. John Duns Scotus was a Scottish Franciscan friar, priest and professor, one of the most important philosopher-theologians of the late medieval West, given the title Doctor Subtilis, “the subtle Doctor,” for the fineness of his reasoning. In the sixteenth century his followers, the Scotists, opposed the Renaissance humanists, and in the mouths of humanists and Reformers “Dunsmen,” “duns” or “dunce” became a term of abuse for one incapable of real scholarship. The OED’s first record is in Tyndale’s Bible of 1530. So the name of the subtlest doctor of the schools became the word for the slowest boy in the class. The Christian observation: the Reformers mocked the schoolmen because their subtlety had run past Scripture. Paul asked, “Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1Co 1:20). He warned against being spoiled “through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8). Yet God’s way of shaming false wisdom is not to honour ignorance: “God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1Co 1:27).
webster_summary: A slow or stupid learner; from the name of John Duns Scotus, the “subtle Doctor,” whose followers the humanists and Reformers mocked (OED earliest 1530, Tyndale). God makes foolish the wisdom of this world (1Co 1:20).
webster_full: DUNCE, n. (from 1530, OED) 1. Originally, a follower of Duns Scotus; a hair-splitting pedant. 2. A person slow at learning; a dullard. From the proper name Duns (John Duns Scotus, c. 1265/66–1308).
History note: Scotists opposed Renaissance humanism, and humanists and Reformers turned their name into a term of abuse (Wikipedia, “Dunce”).
scriptures: Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
Pro 1:22
How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge?
corruption_summary: Dunce is a warning in a word: the subtlest learning of the schools, cut loose from Scripture, ended as a byword for foolishness.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformers did not mock Scotus because he thought too carefully. They mocked a school tradition whose fine distinctions had grown thick enough to hide the plain sense of the Bible. Paul’s warning against philosophy “after the tradition of men… and not after Christ” (Col 2:8) was their charge, and the name of the subtle Doctor became a word for a fool.

The opposite error is just as old: to treat learning itself as the danger and ignorance as piety. Solomon has no praise for the simple who love their simplicity (Pro 1:22). The cure for vain learning is learning that is subject to the word of God.
roots_summary: John Duns Scotus (d. 1308), Doctor Subtilis → Scotists, “Dunsmen” → humanist and Reformer abuse → dunce (OED earliest 1530, Tyndale) → a slow learner.
roots_lines: c. 1265/66–1308: John Duns Scotus, Franciscan friar and theologian, the “subtle Doctor”
1530: OED’s earliest evidence, Tyndale’s Bible
16th century: Scotists oppose the humanists; “dunce” becomes a term of abuse (Wikipedia)
usage: “He was no dunce; he simply never opened the book.”
Hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? (1Co 1:20).

etymology: From a proper name with the suffix -ism, per the Oxford English Dictionary: the Rev. William Archibald Spooner (1844–1930) of New College, Oxford. The OED records its earliest evidence in 1891, in the Western Morning News of Plymouth.
biblical_def: A spoonerism is a slip of the tongue in which the sounds of two words are swapped, as “blushing crow” for “crushing blow.” It is named for William Archibald Spooner, a Church of England clergyman, ordained deacon in 1872 and priest in 1875, chaplain to Archbishop Tait, and for more than sixty years a fellow, dean and warden of New College, Oxford, where he lectured on ancient history, divinity and philosophy. He was known as genial, kindly and hospitable, and famous for absent-mindedness. Most of the spoonerisms told about him were invented by colleagues and students; the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations (1979) accepts only one as genuine, “The weight of rages will press hard upon the employer.” Spooner himself admitted to one: announcing the hymn “The Kinquering Congs Their Titles Take.” The Christian observation: a slip of the tongue is a small thing, and Scripture is realistic about it: “For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man” (Jas 3:2). The prayer for the tongue is the Psalmist’s: “Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips” (Psa 141:3), and “Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight” (Psa 19:14).
webster_summary: A slip in which the sounds of two words are swapped; named for the Rev. W. A. Spooner of Oxford, most of whose famous slips were invented by others (OED earliest 1891). Set a watch before my mouth (Psa 141:3).
webster_full: SPOONERISM, n. (from 1891, OED) An accidental transposition of the initial sounds of two or more words. From the Rev. William Archibald Spooner (1844–1930), warden of New College, Oxford, + -ism.
Note: most spoonerisms attributed to Spooner are apocryphal; one is accepted as genuine (Wikipedia, “Spoonerism”).
scriptures: Jas 3:2
For in many things we offend all. If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.
Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips.
Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer.
O generation of vipers, how can ye, being evil, speak good things? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.
corruption_summary: Spooner is remembered for slips he mostly never made; the lesson is how easily a good man’s name is carried off by stories told for a laugh.
corruption_paragraphs: A slip of the tongue is no sin, and the laughter it brings can be innocent. Spooner’s own one admitted slip, in announcing a hymn, harmed no one. But the legend that grew around him is made almost entirely of stories that other men invented and fastened to his name.

That is a small instance of a serious habit. A good name is easily spent on someone else’s joke. Christ said the mouth speaks out of the abundance of the heart (Mat 12:34); the man who repeats a story about his neighbour should know whether it is true.
roots_summary: Rev. William Archibald Spooner (1844–1930), New College, Oxford → slips attributed to him → spoonerism (OED earliest 1891).
roots_lines: 1872 deacon, 1875 priest, Church of England; 1903–1924 warden of New College (Wikipedia)
1891: OED’s earliest evidence, Western Morning News (Plymouth)
Genuine example accepted by the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations: “The weight of rages”
usage: “He meant ‘crushing blow’ and said ‘blushing crow,’ a perfect spoonerism.”
Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips. (Psa 141:3).

etymology: From a proper name, per the Oxford English Dictionary: Louis Braille (1809–1852), the French teacher of the blind who invented the system. The OED records its earliest evidence in 1853, in the writing of E. C. Johnson, the year after Braille’s death.
biblical_def: Braille is the system of raised dots, read by touch, by which the blind read and write. Its inventor, Louis Braille, was blinded as a small child: at three he injured an eye with a stitching awl in his father’s harness-making shop, infection spread, and by five he was completely blind. He won a scholarship to the Royal Institute for Blind Youth in Paris, where the books embossed raised Latin letters that had to be traced slowly. Learning of a raised-dot system devised by Charles Barbier, he simplified it to cells of six dots that a fingertip could read at a single touch, and published it in 1829. He later taught at the Institute. A devout Catholic, he was also an accomplished organist and played for churches in Paris. The Christian observation: Scripture does not treat blindness as a curse to be hidden. Christ said of the man born blind, “Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him” (Joh 9:3). “The LORD openeth the eyes of the blind” (Psa 146:8), and among the signs that He was the Christ, “the blind see” (Luk 7:22). Braille’s dots let the blind read the Scriptures with their own hands until that day when “the eyes of the blind shall be opened” (Isa 35:5).
webster_summary: A system of raised dots read by touch, invented by Louis Braille, blind from childhood (OED earliest 1853). The LORD openeth the eyes of the blind (Psa 146:8).
webster_full: BRAILLE, n. (from 1853, OED) A system of writing and printing for the blind in which characters are formed by patterns of raised dots in cells of six, read by touch. From Louis Braille (1809–1852).
History note: adapted from Charles Barbier’s raised-dot system; first published in 1829 (Wikipedia, “Louis Braille”).
scriptures: Joh 9:3
Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.
The LORD openeth the eyes of the blind: the LORD raiseth them that are bowed down: the LORD loveth the righteous:
Luk 7:22

Then Jesus answering said unto them, Go your way, and tell John what things ye have seen and heard; how that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, to the poor the gospel is preached.
Isa 35:5
Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped.
corruption_summary: Braille’s life answers the old lie that affliction is always punishment; Christ said the man born blind was blind that the works of God should be shown in him.
corruption_paragraphs: The disciples assumed that blindness meant someone’s sin: “who did sin, this man, or his parents?” Christ refused the assumption (Joh 9:3). The same assumption survives in quieter forms, in the habit of treating the disabled as burdens or as lives of lesser worth.

Louis Braille, blind from the age of five, gave the blind of the world the power to read for themselves. The work of God was made manifest in him in a way his sighted teachers had not managed. The church should see every afflicted life the same way, as a place where God intends to work.
roots_summary: Louis Braille (1809–1852), blind from childhood → six-dot cell adapted from Barbier, published 1829 → braille (OED earliest 1853).
roots_lines: Age three: injured with a stitching awl; completely blind by five (Wikipedia)
1829: first publication of his system (Wikipedia)
1853: OED’s earliest evidence, E. C. Johnson
usage: “Her grandmother read the Psalms from a braille Bible.”
The LORD openeth the eyes of the blind. (Psa 146:8).

etymology: From a proper name, per the Oxford English Dictionary: Guy Fawkes (1570–1606), of the Gunpowder Plot of 1605. The OED records its earliest evidence for this noun in 1796, in the Oracle.
biblical_def: A guy first meant an effigy of Guy Fawkes, carried through the streets and burned on the fifth of November; it then came to mean a grotesquely dressed person, and in America simply a man or fellow. Guy Fawkes was one of a group of English Catholics in the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, which planned to blow up the House of Lords, assassinate King James I and restore a Catholic monarch. Fawkes was put in charge of the gunpowder stockpiled in an undercroft beneath the House of Lords. An anonymous letter warned the authorities, and he was caught. The day of deliverance became Guy Fawkes Night; toward the end of the eighteenth century children began begging for money with effigies of Fawkes, and the effigy became the “guy.” The Christian observation: Scripture forbids exactly what the plotters attempted. “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1); “My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change” (Pro 24:21). David prayed for deliverance “from the secret counsel of the wicked; from the insurrection of the workers of iniquity” (Psa 64:2). And the believer who is wronged is told, “avenge not yourselves” (Rom 12:19).
webster_summary: Originally an effigy of Guy Fawkes, of the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, burned on the fifth of November (OED earliest 1796); hence a man or fellow. Deliverance from the secret counsel of the wicked (Psa 64:2).
webster_full: GUY, n. (from 1796, OED) 1. An effigy of Guy Fawkes, paraded and burned on 5 November. 2. A grotesquely dressed person. 3. (U.S., colloquial) A man; a fellow. From the proper name Guy Fawkes.
History note: the Gunpowder Plot of 1605 aimed to blow up the House of Lords and kill James I (Wikipedia, “Guy Fawkes”).
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change:
Psa 64:2
Hide me from the secret counsel of the wicked; from the insurrection of the workers of iniquity:
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: Fawkes’s name went from a would-be assassin to a burning effigy to the most casual word for a man; the forgetting is the warning, because a nation that forgets its deliverances forgets who delivered it.
corruption_paragraphs: Few who say “you guys” know that the word began with a man who meant to blow up a king and his Parliament. The plot was real, the deliverance was real, and for generations the day was kept as a thanksgiving. Over time the festival drifted into bonfires and mischief, and the name into slang.

Scripture commands God’s people to remember His deliverances and tell them to their children. It also condemns the means the plotters chose: secret violence against the ruling powers (Rom 13:1; Psa 64:2). Zeal for a cause, however sincere, does not license murder.
roots_summary: Guy Fawkes (1570–1606), Gunpowder Plot 1605 → 5 November effigies → guy (OED earliest 1796) → oddly dressed person → U.S. “a fellow.”
roots_lines: 1605: the Gunpowder Plot discovered after an anonymous letter (Wikipedia)
Late 18th century: children beg for money with effigies of Fawkes (Wikipedia, “Guy Fawkes Night”)
1796: OED’s earliest evidence, Oracle
usage: “The boys built a guy for the bonfire on the fifth of November.”
Hide me from the secret counsel of the wicked. (Psa 64:2).

etymology: From a proper name, per the Oxford English Dictionary: Pandarus, the go-between in the medieval story of Troilus and Criseyde. The OED records its earliest evidence from around 1450. The noun comes from Chaucer’s use of the character, the verb from Shakespeare’s.
biblical_def: A pander is one who procures for the lusts of others; to pander is to act as one, and now, more loosely, to indulge or cater to someone’s lower appetites. The name comes from Pandarus. In Homer’s Iliad he is a Trojan archer who breaks a truce. In medieval literature he becomes the witty, licentious figure who arranges the affair between Troilus and Criseyde, in Geoffrey Chaucer’s Troilus and Criseyde (1370s) and later in Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida. From Chaucer comes the noun pander; from Shakespeare, the verb. The Christian observation: Proverbs gives the pander’s method and the answer to it. “With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him” (Pro 7:21); the counsel is “Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house” (Pro 5:8). Paul warned of those who “creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins” (2Ti 3:6). The Christian is to “have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them” (Eph 5:11).
webster_summary: A go-between in vice, from Pandarus of the Troilus story (OED around 1450); to pander is to cater to lower appetites. Come not nigh the door of her house (Pro 5:8).
webster_full: PANDER, n. (from around 1450, OED) A go-between in illicit love; a procurer. v. To act as a pander; to indulge or cater to another’s base desires. From the proper name Pandarus.
Literary note: the noun from Chaucer’s Troilus and Criseyde, the verb from Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida (Wikipedia, “Pandarus”).
scriptures: Pro 7:21
With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.
Pro 5:8
Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house:
For of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, led away with divers lusts,
Eph 5:11
And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.
corruption_summary: The old pander arranged sin for one client at a time; the corruption now is an economy that panders to lust at scale and calls it entertainment or free choice.
corruption_paragraphs: Pandarus was a single go-between with a single purpose. The modern market has made his trade into an industry. Advertising, entertainment and the screen in every pocket cater to the lower appetites because those appetites sell, and the word pander has softened to mean only giving people what they want.

Scripture does not treat the go-between as innocent because the parties were willing. The one who leads others into sin shares the sin. Proverbs counsels distance, not management: come not nigh the door (Pro 5:8). The Christian father guards his house against the panders who creep in (2Ti 3:6).
roots_summary: Pandarus (Homer’s archer; medieval go-between) → Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde → pander n. (OED around 1450) → Shakespeare, verb pander.
roots_lines: Iliad Book 4: Pandarus breaks the truce with an arrow (Wikipedia)
Chaucer, Troilus and Criseyde: Pandarus as go-between (Wikipedia)
Around 1450: OED’s earliest evidence for pander
usage: “The network pandered to the worst in its audience and called it ratings.”
Remove thy way far from her, and come not nigh the door of her house. (Pro 5:8).

etymology: From a proper name with the suffix -an, per the Oxford English Dictionary: Procrustes, the bandit of Greek legend. The OED records its earliest evidence in 1647, in the writing of John Goodwin, Independent minister. The Greek name means “the stretcher.”
biblical_def: Procrustean describes a rule that forces everyone to fit a single arbitrary standard, whatever harm it does. In Greek legend Procrustes, “the stretcher,” was a rogue smith and bandit of Attica who kept a stronghold on the sacred way between Athens and Eleusis. He offered every passer-by a bed for the night, then made him fit it: if the guest was too short, he stretched him with his smith’s hammer; if too tall, he cut off the excess. Nobody ever fit the bed exactly, until Theseus killed him. The word’s first English use the OED records is by a Puritan minister, John Goodwin, in 1647. The Christian observation: Christ condemned the religious Procrusteans of His day. “For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers” (Mat 23:4; Luk 11:46). The church’s standard is not a bed of man’s making but God’s word. And the world has its own Procrustean bed, against which Paul warns: “be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Rom 12:2).
webster_summary: Forcing conformity to an arbitrary standard regardless of harm; from Procrustes, who stretched or cut his guests to fit his bed (OED earliest 1647). Heavy burdens laid on men’s shoulders (Mat 23:4).
webster_full: PROCRUSTEAN, adj. (from 1647, OED) Enforcing uniformity by violent or arbitrary means; tailoring facts or persons to fit a preconceived scheme. From Procrustes + -an.
Legend note: Procrustes stretched or amputated his guests to fit an iron bed (Wikipedia, “Procrustes”).
scriptures: Mat 23:4
For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers.
And he said, Woe unto you also, ye lawyers! for ye lade men with burdens grievous to be borne, and ye yourselves touch not the burdens with one of your fingers.
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
corruption_summary: A Procrustean rule makes men fit the bed; the corruption is any authority, in church or state, that binds a man-made standard on consciences as if it were God’s law.
corruption_paragraphs: Procrustes’ crime was not that he had a standard but that the standard was his own and he enforced it by maiming. Religious legalism works the same way: rules invented by men are laid on consciences, and those who do not fit are stretched or cut until they do (Mat 23:4).

The modern state and the modern market have their own beds, and the pressure to conform to them is relentless (Rom 12:2). The Christian answer is not the absence of a standard but the right one: the word of God, applied to men in the spirit of meekness (Gal 6:1), which restores instead of mutilating.
roots_summary: Greek Prokroustēs, “the stretcher” → the bandit and his bed → Procrustean (OED earliest 1647, John Goodwin) → arbitrary forced conformity.
roots_lines: Legend: a bandit of Attica on the sacred way between Athens and Eleusis, killed by Theseus (Wikipedia)
1647: OED’s earliest evidence, John Goodwin, Independent minister
usage: “The new curriculum was a Procrustean bed: every child cut to the same length.”
Be not conformed to this world. (Rom 12:2).

etymology: From a proper name, per the Oxford English Dictionary: FitzRoy Somerset, 1st Baron Raglan (1788–1855). The OED records its earliest evidence in 1854, in the Ipswich Journal, the year Raglan took command in the Crimea.
biblical_def: A raglan is a sleeve that runs in one piece all the way to the collar, with a diagonal seam from underarm to collarbone, or a coat cut that way. It is named for Lord Raglan. As a young officer FitzRoy Somerset served in the Peninsular War and the Waterloo campaign as military secretary to the Duke of Wellington. At Waterloo in 1815 his right arm was amputated, and he then demanded the arm back so that he could recover the ring his wife had given him. Finding it hard to dress after the amputation, he is credited with the sleeve sewn from the collar rather than the shoulder. He later commanded the British troops sent to the Crimea in 1854, and died in 1855. The Christian observation: the raglan sleeve is a small gift born of a wound, and Scripture is full of that pattern. The faithful man is not told his wounds will be spared him, but that God works through them: “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might” (Ecc 9:10). A ring kept from a severed hand is a picture of covenant faithfulness under suffering. “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2Co 12:9).
webster_summary: A sleeve running in one piece to the collar, or a coat so cut; named for Lord Raglan, who lost his right arm at Waterloo (OED earliest 1854). Strength made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9).
webster_full: RAGLAN, n. and adj. (from 1854, OED) A sleeve extending in one piece to the collar, with a diagonal seam from underarm to collarbone; a coat with such sleeves. From FitzRoy Somerset, 1st Baron Raglan (1788–1855).
History note: Raglan lost his right arm at Waterloo; the sleeve is credited to his difficulty in dressing afterward (Wikipedia).
scriptures: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Ecc 9:10
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength.
corruption_summary: The raglan shows a wounded man adapting and carrying on; the error of our age is to treat every weakness as the end of usefulness instead of the place where God’s strength is shown.
corruption_paragraphs: Raglan lost his sword arm at Waterloo and served another forty years, adapting even his coat to the loss. The culture prizes wholeness and strength, and tends to count the wounded and the weak as finished.

Paul gloried in his infirmities, that the power of Christ might rest on him (2Co 12:9). No man is saved by his own strength (Psa 33:16); the wounded veteran who keeps serving is a better sermon on that than many preachers.
roots_summary: FitzRoy Somerset, 1st Baron Raglan → right arm amputated at Waterloo, 1815 → sleeve sewn from the collar → raglan (OED earliest 1854).
roots_lines: 1815: right arm amputated at Waterloo; recovers his wife’s ring (Wikipedia)
1854: commands British troops in the Crimea; OED’s earliest evidence, Ipswich Journal
28 June 1855: dies (Wikipedia)
usage: “The raglan sleeves gave him room to swing the axe.”
My strength is made perfect in weakness. (2Co 12:9).

etymology: From a proper name, per the Oxford English Dictionary: James Watt (1736–1819), the Scottish engineer. The OED records its earliest evidence in 1882, in the writing of C. W. Siemens, who proposed the name for the unit that year in his presidential address to the British Association for the Advancement of Science.
biblical_def: The watt is the unit of power, one joule per second: the rate at which energy is used or delivered. It is named for James Watt, a Scottish inventor, engineer and chemist. While working as an instrument maker at the University of Glasgow he saw that Thomas Newcomen’s steam engine wasted energy by repeatedly cooling and reheating its cylinder, and he added a separate condenser, which greatly improved its power, efficiency and cost. His engine of 1776, later adapted to rotary motion, was fundamental to the Industrial Revolution. Watt also developed the idea of horsepower. In 1882 C. William Siemens proposed naming a unit after him, and in 1960 the General Conference on Weights and Measures adopted the watt into the International System of Units. The Christian observation: the measure of power is named for a man who found the waste in a machine and stopped it. Scripture commends that kind of skill: “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings” (Pro 22:29). But it also reminds us whose power the engines borrow. God “telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names” (Psa 147:4), and “power belongeth unto God” (Psa 62:11).
webster_summary: The SI unit of power, one joule per second; named for James Watt, who added the separate condenser to the steam engine (OED earliest 1882). Power belongeth unto God (Psa 62:11).
webster_full: WATT, n. (from 1882, OED) The SI unit of power, equal to one joule per second. From James Watt (1736–1819).
History note: the name was proposed by C. W. Siemens in 1882; adopted into the SI in 1960 (Wikipedia, “Watt”).
scriptures: Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names.
God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God.
corruption_summary: We measure power in watts and forget that every watt is borrowed from a creation God made and sustains; the industrial age’s temptation is to think power is ours.
corruption_paragraphs: Watt’s engine multiplied what one man could do, and the age it began has multiplied it many times since. It is easy for a people with power at the flick of a switch to think the power is their own achievement.

Scripture says otherwise: power belongs to God (Psa 62:11), and the heat, coal and current that run our machines are His creation. Skill like Watt’s is to be honoured (Pro 22:29); the power itself is to be received with thanks and used as stewards.
roots_summary: James Watt (1736–1819), separate condenser, steam engine of 1776 → Siemens proposes the unit, 1882 → watt (OED earliest 1882) → SI unit of power, 1960.
roots_lines: 1776: Watt’s improved steam engine (Wikipedia)
1882: C. W. Siemens proposes the name; OED’s earliest evidence
1960: adopted into the International System of Units (Wikipedia)
usage: “Swap the hundred-watt bulb for something dimmer in the nursery.”

etymology: From a proper name with the suffix -an, per the Oxford English Dictionary: Martin Luther. The OED records its earliest evidence in 1521, in a letter by W. Warham. The name began as a term of abuse: Johann Maier von Eck used it against Luther at the Leipzig Debate in July 1519, following the practice of naming a heresy after its leader.
biblical_def: A Lutheran is a member of the branch of the Protestant church that arose from the work of Martin Luther, the German friar and Reformer whose efforts, beginning with the Ninety-five Theses of 1517, helped launch the Reformation. Lutheran churches adhere to the Bible and the ecumenical creeds, with their doctrine set out in the Book of Concord. The name was not chosen by Luther’s followers. It was pinned on them by his opponent Johann Eck at the Leipzig Debate in 1519, on the old principle that a heresy is named after its founder; many Lutherans have preferred the name evangelical. The Christian observation: the Reformation’s recovery was of Scripture, not of a man. Its heart is Paul’s: “For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith” (Rom 1:17), and “a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16). Paul himself rebuked the factions that took men’s names: “every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos… Is Christ divided?” (1Co 1:12–13).
webster_summary: Of the Protestant church that arose from Martin Luther’s Reformation; a member of it. The name began as a slur by Johann Eck in 1519 (OED earliest 1521). The just shall live by faith (Rom 1:17).
webster_full: LUTHERAN, adj. and n. (from 1521, OED) Of or relating to Martin Luther or the churches holding his teaching; a member of such a church. From the proper name Luther + -an.
History note: first used as a derogatory label by Johann Eck at the Leipzig Debate, July 1519 (Wikipedia, “Lutheranism”).

corruption_summary: Lutheran was coined to brand the gospel as one man’s heresy; the name stuck, and the danger since has been to honour the man and lose the gospel he preached.
corruption_paragraphs: Eck’s tactic was to make the recovery of justification by faith look like one friar’s novelty. If it was Luther’s, it was not Paul’s. The Reformers answered by pointing every claim back to Scripture (Rom 1:17; Gal 2:16).

Paul’s rebuke of the Corinthian factions (1Co 1:12–13) cuts both ways. Protestants may honour Luther as a faithful servant, but no one was baptized into his name. A church that keeps his name while losing the doctrine of justification has kept the slur and thrown away the gospel.
roots_summary: Martin Luther → Ninety-five Theses, 1517 → Eck’s slur at Leipzig, 1519 → Lutheran (OED earliest 1521) → name of a communion.
